findings.title: Default authz-client crypto provider throws UnsupportedOperationException for standard operations
findings.body: The service file registers AuthzClientCryptoProvider, and CryptoIntegration now selects providers automatically, so a standalone authz-client classpath with only this provider will use it as the active CryptoProvider. However many methods required by Keycloak JOSE/client-credential flows are implemented as `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.")`, including getSignature() at line 218. For example, signed-JWT client authentication uses JWSBuilder, which calls CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getSignature(...), so it will fail at runtime. This breaks existing authz-client functionality for private_key_jwt/signed client assertions.

findings.title: Removing the multiple-provider error can silently bypass FIPS provider selection
findings.body: detectProvider() now sorts providers by order instead of throwing when more than one provider is present. But DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return the same order value (200). If a FIPS distribution accidentally also contains keycloak-crypto-default, the first provider among equal order values will be chosen based on undefined ServiceLoader/resource ordering rather than an explicit FIPS decision. This can silently select the non-FIPS DefaultCryptoProvider and violate FIPS mode.

findings.title: Adding abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider is a public interface, but this change adds a new abstract method `int order()` without a default implementation. Existing third-party or downstream implementations of CryptoProvider will fail to compile against this version, and already-compiled implementations will fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError when loaded through ServiceLoader. A default method with a predictable default order would preserve compatibility.

findings.title: ES384/ES512 tests reuse the same default EC key pair and do not verify signatures
findings.body: The constructor generates a single EC key pair with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")`, which normally uses the default curve (secp256r1/P-256). The same key pair is then used for testES256(), testES384(), and testES512(). The test only round-trips DER<->concatenated R/S encoding using the requested signLength and never verifies a signature, so ES384 and ES512 conversions are not actually validated against an appropriate P-384/P-521 key and incorrect curve-specific behavior can pass unnoticed.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default KeyStore provider, not BouncyCastle
findings.body: The method `getBouncyCastleProvider()` is documented and used as an accessor for a BouncyCastle-compatible Provider, but this implementation returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, usually SUN/SunJCE. Any code that expects BC-specific algorithms or casts/uses this provider as BouncyCastle will get the wrong provider and may fail or silently use unintended cryptography.
